43.title: The overflowing cup
43.hook: the master Nan-in pours tea for a professor until it spills: you are already full (Zen story, Japan)
43.howItsDone: Zen teachers often begin with beginner's mind, shoshin, and the cup of tea story is widely told in Zen centers and far beyond them to describe coming to practice without assuming you already understand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the guard searched the straw for years, and the answer was the donkey. Your line was it's the donkey. What obvious thing did you finally see? Day forty-three, and a new week: Zen stories.
screen: `IT'S THE DONKEY.`

segments.voice: Picture a quiet room in Japan, a little over a hundred years ago. A university professor has come to visit a Zen master named Nan-in. He wants to learn about Zen, and he has a lot to say about it. He's read the books. He has theories. He talks, and talks. Nan-in says almost nothing. He just makes tea. He sets a cup in front of the professor, lifts the pot, and begins to pour. The cup fills to the brim. And Nan-in keeps pouring. Tea runs over the rim, across the table, onto the floor. Today's story is the overflowing cup.
screen: `A PROFESSOR COMES TO LEARN.` → `HE TALKS, AND TALKS.` → `THE MASTER KEEPS POURING.`

segments.voice: The professor can't stand it. Stop, he says, it's full! Nothing more will go in! And Nan-in puts the pot down. That's you, he says, more or less. You're like this cup: full of your own opinions. How can I show you anything, until you empty it first? That's the whole story, and it has traveled around the world. You'll find it on posters, in business books, in yoga studios. A word about where it comes from. It's told as a story about a Japanese master of the Meiji era, the late eighteen hundreds. But most of us know it from a small English collection of Zen stories published in the 1950s, and its earlier history is hard to trace. So hold it as a teaching story, not a court record. What it teaches is simple and hard. You can't learn what you think you already know. The professor didn't come to learn. He came to be confirmed. Every new thing Nan-in might have said would have spilled off the top of what was already there. Zen has a word for the opposite state: shoshin, beginner's mind. The Japanese teacher Shunryu Suzuki made it famous in America, teaching that a beginner sees many possibilities where an expert sees few. Emptying the cup doesn't mean throwing away everything you know. It means leaving room. Room for the other person to surprise you. Room for a subject you think you've mastered to still have something to say. The cup is only useful for the space inside it.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pour a cup slowly, watching the level. If you have a cup and some water nearby, try it now, or picture it. Pour slowly. Watch the level rise. Notice the moment just before full, when there's still a little room. Stop there. Then sit with that cup in front of you, and breathe. Think of one subject, or one person, you're sure you already understand. Leave a little room at the top. The bell holds the time.

44.title: Two monks and a river
44.hook: Tanzan carries a woman across a stream, and hours later Ekido is still carrying her in his head (Zen story, Japan)
44.carry: I set her down at the river
44.howItsDone: Zen teachers often tell the story of Tanzan and Ekido when talking about letting go, and in meditation practice people notice a thought they keep returning to and set it down, again and again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nan-in poured tea until it spilled. Your line was empty the cup. Did you listen once today as if you knew nothing yet? Day forty-four.

segments.voice: It's two in the morning, and you're replaying something someone said to you at lunch. Or last week. Or in 2019. They've long forgotten it. They're asleep. And you're still turning it over, holding it, carrying it around the dark room. Everybody knows that feeling. Today's story is about two monks walking home in the rain. Their names were Tanzan and Ekido. The water is high and the road is a mess, and at the crossing stands a young woman in a silk kimono who can't get across. Tanzan does something that his companion will not stop thinking about for hours. Today's story is two monks and a river.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING, REPLAYING.` → `TANZAN AND EKIDO.` → `A WOMAN WHO CAN'T CROSS.`

segments.voice: Tanzan doesn't hesitate. Come on, he says. He picks her up in his arms, carries her across the water, sets her down on the other side, and walks on. Ekido says nothing. Not a word, all afternoon, all the way to the temple. But he's boiling. These monks had vowed to keep their distance from women, and his companion just picked one up in the road. Finally, that night, he can't hold it in. We monks aren't supposed to go near women, he says. Especially not young and lovely ones. Why did you do that? And Tanzan answers: I set her down at the river. Are you still carrying her? That's the story. A word on the details: in the oldest English telling, the crossing is a flooded, muddy road; most retellings made it a river, and the river stuck. Tanzan was a real Zen teacher of nineteenth-century Japan, known for being unconventional. Now look who's really carrying the woman. Tanzan held her for a minute, to help, and let her go. Ekido never touched her, and he carried her for hours, in his head, heavier with every step. The weight wasn't in the act. It was in the holding on. That's why this story gets told at kitchen tables and in therapists' offices. The old insult. The awkward moment. The thing you should have said. The thing that was done, and finished, long ago. Zen teachers have a word for letting go, hōge, casting down. The question is Tanzan's: are you still carrying her?

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set down one thing you're still carrying. Settle, and breathe. Find something that happened, and is over, but that you're still holding. A remark. A mistake. An argument that ended days ago. Feel where you carry it: shoulders, jaw, stomach. Now picture a river. Picture yourself walking to the far bank, and setting it down on the ground there. You don't have to forget it. Just stop carrying it for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.

45.title: Is that so?
45.hook: Hakuin is wrongly blamed for a child, raises him, is later cleared, and says only "is that so?" (Zen story, Japan)
45.howItsDone: Zen teachers tell the story of Hakuin's "is that so?" to describe equanimity, meeting praise and blame alike, and Hakuin himself is honored in Japanese Rinzai Zen as the teacher who renewed it.

screen: `DAY FORTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tanzan carried a woman across the water and set her down, and Ekido carried her all day. Your line was I set her down at the river. What did you put down? Day forty-five.

segments.voice: Think about the last time someone got you wrong. A rumor at work. A friend who believed the worst. A comment online from someone who'd never met you. Remember the heat in your face, and the speech you wrote in your head: let me explain, you don't understand, how dare you. Now meet Hakuin. He was one of the great Zen masters of Japan, in the seventeen hundreds, a teacher and painter still honored today. And the story told about him is this. One morning, angry parents bang on his door, holding a newborn baby, and they accuse him of something he never did. Today's story is is that so?
screen: `SOMEONE GOT YOU WRONG.` → `LET ME EXPLAIN!` → `HAKUIN AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's how it's told. A young woman in the village is pregnant, and won't say who the father is. Her parents press her, and finally she names Hakuin, the monk up the road. When the baby is born, the furious parents carry it to his door. This is yours, they say. Take it. And Hakuin says only: is that so? He takes the baby. His good name is gone. People who bowed to him in the road now look away. He asks the neighbors for milk, and cares for the child. He doesn't argue, doesn't explain. A year later, the young mother can't bear it anymore. She tells her parents the truth: the father is a young man who works at the fish market. Now the parents run back up the road, full of shame, apologizing, begging to take the child home. Hakuin hands the baby back. And he says: is that so? Nobody can say for certain this happened; it's a story told about Hakuin, not a record. But look at what those three words do. They aren't agreement: he never says yes, it's mine. And they aren't a fight. They just receive the news. Is that so. Blame arrives, and he meets it the same way he meets praise. And in between, the thing that needed doing, caring for a baby, got done. We mostly spend our energy on the story about us. Hakuin spent his on the child in front of him. That's the hard part, and the free part.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: meet one piece of news with is that so. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something someone said about you, fair or unfair, praise or blame. Notice what your body does with it: the rush to defend, or the glow of being liked. Now say inside, slowly: is that so. Not yes. Not no. Just is that so. Let the words take the heat out. Then turn your attention to one thing in front of you that needs care. The bell holds the time.

46.title: The moon can't be stolen
46.hook: the hermit Ryokan gives a thief his clothes and wishes he could give him the moon (Zen story, Japan)
46.howItsDone: Ryokan is loved in Japan as a poet-monk of simple living, and Zen teachers often tell the story of the thief and the moon when talking about generosity and letting go of possessions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hakuin met blame and apology with the same three words. Your line was is that so. When did you say it inside? Day forty-six.

segments.voice: Picture the smallest home you can imagine. One room. A straw roof. A bowl, a cushion, a few poems written on scraps of paper. That was the hut of Ryokan, a Zen monk and poet who lived alone at the foot of a mountain in Japan, around the year 1800. He played with the village children, begged for his rice, and wrote some of the most loved poems in the Japanese language. One evening, while Ryokan is out walking, a thief slips into the hut, looking for something to steal. There is nothing. Then Ryokan comes home, and finds him. Today's story is the moon can't be stolen.
screen: `ONE ROOM, A STRAW ROOF.` → `RYOKAN, MONK AND POET.` → `A THIEF IN THE EMPTY HUT.`

segments.voice: The thief is caught. And Ryokan isn't angry. He's sorry. You've come such a long way to visit me, he says, and you shouldn't go home empty-handed. Please, take my clothes. And he takes off the robe he's wearing and hands it over. The thief, bewildered, grabs the clothes and runs off into the dark. Ryokan sits down, naked, in his doorway, and looks up at the night. The moon is rising, huge and bright. And he says to himself: poor fellow. I wish I could have given him this beautiful moon. The story is usually tied to a short poem that Japanese tradition credits to Ryokan: the thief left it behind, the moon in my window. Scholars can't say for sure the robbery happened just this way, but the poem and the story have traveled together for a long time. Now look at what Ryokan knows. The thief came for things. Ryokan barely had any, and gave away the last of them without a fight. What he actually treasured, the thief couldn't carry off, because it wasn't his to keep in the first place. The moon doesn't belong to anyone. It shines on the hut and the thief's road the same. Ryokan's wish is the whole teaching: he wants the thief to have what he himself has. Not the robe. The seeing. The quiet. A night bright enough to be rich in. We guard our things carefully, and they can be lost. The moon stays.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give one thing freely today. For now, settle, and breathe. Think of something you have that no one could steal: a view you love, a memory, a skill, the fact that you're breathing. Rest in it for a moment. Then think of one small thing you could give away today, with nothing asked back. A coat you don't wear. Your time. A kind word to someone who didn't earn it. Picture handing it over, the way Ryokan does, and letting it go. The bell holds the time.
The moon can't be stolen. Ryokan gives a thief his clothes, and wishes he could give him the moon. Today's word.

47.title: Wash your bowl
47.hook: a new monk asks for teaching, Zhaozhou asks if he's eaten, and says: then wash your bowl (Gateless Gate, case 7)
47.howItsDone: In Zen monasteries, meals are eaten in silence from a set of nested bowls that each monk cleans at the table, and daily work like cooking and cleaning is treated as part of practice, not a break from it.

segments.voice: You've finally done it. You signed up for the class, joined the gym, opened the book everyone talks about. And on the first day you walk in ready for the big secret. Tell me the thing. The real thing. The key. Now picture a young monk in China, more than a thousand years ago, doing exactly that. He's just entered the monastery. He finds the old master, Zhaozhou, one of the most famous teachers in the history of Zen, and he asks, earnestly: I've just arrived. Please, teach me. And Zhaozhou asks him about breakfast. Today's story is wash your bowl.
screen: `TELL ME THE REAL THING.` → `A NEW MONK ARRIVES.` → `PLEASE, TEACH ME.`

segments.voice: This one comes from a real book: the Gateless Gate, a collection of forty-eight short Zen cases gathered in China in the twelve hundreds by a monk named Wumen. It's case seven, and it's only a few lines long. The monk says: I've just entered the monastery. Please teach me. Zhaozhou asks: have you eaten your rice porridge? The monk says: yes, I have. And Zhaozhou says: then wash your bowl. The book says the monk understood. That's it. No lecture. No secret. The monk wanted something special, and Zhaozhou pointed him at the dishes. Here's what makes it more than a brush-off. In a Zen monastery, washing your bowl isn't a chore you do before the practice starts. It is the practice. Eat when you eat. Wash when you wash. Do the next plain thing completely, with your whole attention, instead of reaching past it for something grander. The teaching isn't hidden somewhere else. It's in your hands, in the warm water, in the bowl. Zen kept saying this, in many voices. The Japanese teacher Dogen, who studied in China and came home in 1227, wrote a whole set of instructions for the monastery cook, and treated washing rice and scrubbing pots as seriously as sitting in the meditation hall. And notice what Zhaozhou didn't say. He didn't call the porridge unimportant, or tell the monk to hurry past breakfast to reach the real teaching. He sent him back to the bowl he'd just used. You don't need a mountain or a retreat. You have a sink, and one dish. That's enough.

48.title: The finger and the moon
48.hook: a teaching points at something, so don't stare at the pointing finger (a Buddhist image, Surangama Sutra, much used in Zen)
48.howItsDone: Zen teachers often use the finger and the moon to remind students that sutras, koans and talks point toward direct experience, and many Zen schools pair careful study with sitting practice for that reason.

segments.voice: Try this with a very young baby. Point at a ball across the room. Often the baby looks at your finger. Grabs it, even. The ball sits there, ignored, and the baby stares at your hand, waiting for it to do something. It's sweet in a baby. It's less funny when we do it. And we do it all the time. There's a picture for this, a well-loved one in the Buddhist world, and Zen teachers have used it for many centuries. Someone points at the moon. And the other person looks at the finger. Today's story is the finger and the moon.
screen: `POINT AT THE BALL.` → `THE BABY LOOKS AT YOUR FINGER.` → `SOMEONE POINTS AT THE MOON.`

segments.voice: The picture appears in a Mahayana Buddhist scripture called the Surangama Sutra. The Buddha is talking with his cousin and attendant Ananda, who has heard a great many teachings and remembers every word. And the Buddha tells him, more or less: when someone points at the moon to show it to you, you should follow the finger and look at the moon. If you look at the finger and take it for the moon, you lose the moon. And you lose the finger too, because you've mistaken what a finger is for. That last part is sharp. It's not just that you miss the moon. You also misunderstand the pointing. A finger is for looking past. Zen took this image and ran with it. A famous old story tells of the teacher Huineng, who couldn't read, being asked by a nun how he could understand scriptures he couldn't even read. And he answers with this picture: the truth is like the moon, and words are like a finger. You can see the moon without the finger. Here's why it matters beyond Zen. Every teaching points. Words, books, rituals, even these lessons. They're fingers. They are precious, and worth studying, and they are not the thing. The danger is falling in love with the pointing: memorizing the words, arguing about the finger's shape, collecting fingers. And missing the moon, which is right there, and was the point. So when you hear a teaching, ask: what is this pointing at? Then look there.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the sky, not the screen. When the bell starts, put this phone face down, and if you can, go to a window or step outside. Look up. Whatever's there: clouds, blue, gray, the moon if you're lucky, a ceiling if that's all there is. This lesson was the finger. The sky is the moon. Just look. Let it be bigger than anything you've read today. The bell holds the time.
The finger and the moon. Teachings point beyond themselves; don't stare at the finger and miss the moon. Today's word.

49.title: The strawberry
49.hook: chased by a tiger, hanging from a vine over another tiger, a man tastes a wild strawberry (Buddhist parable, as retold in Zen)
49.howItsDone: Zen teachers retell the strawberry parable to point at full attention in the present moment, and mindful eating, tasting one small thing slowly, is a common practice in many meditation settings.

screen: `DAY FORTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, someone pointed at the moon, and we tried not to stare at the finger. Your line was not the finger. Did you look up at the sky? Day forty-nine, the last of the Zen week.
screen: `NOT THE FINGER.`

segments.voice: A man is walking across a field when he hears it: a growl. A tiger, coming fast. He runs. He reaches the edge of a cliff, grabs the root of a wild vine, and swings himself over the edge. For a moment he's safe. He hangs there, breathing hard. The tiger paces above him, sniffing. He looks down. Far below, a second tiger is waiting for him to fall. And then two mice, one white and one black, come out and begin, little by little, to gnaw through the vine. Today's story is the strawberry.
screen: `A TIGER, COMING FAST.` → `A VINE OVER THE CLIFF.` → `TWO MICE, GNAWING.`

segments.voice: And then he sees it. Growing out of the cliff face, just within reach: a wild strawberry, red and ripe. Holding the vine with one hand, he reaches out with the other and picks it. And the story ends: how sweet it tasted! That's the Zen telling, and it stops right there, on the sweetness, without rescuing him. The story is much older than Zen. An ancient Indian parable tells of a man hanging in a well over a monster, with honey dripping into his mouth. It appears in Buddhist writings, in the great Hindu epic the Mahabharata, and it traveled west too, into medieval Christian stories. Most versions read it as a warning: the mice are day and night, eating through our time, and the honey is the pleasure that distracts us from our danger. The Zen retelling turns it around. The tigers are still there. The mice still gnaw. Nothing is fixed. But in the middle of all that, there is a strawberry, and he tastes it completely. Not in spite of the danger, and not by ignoring it. Right there, knowing. Each of us is on the vine. Nobody gets off the cliff. We could spend the whole time staring up at one tiger and down at the other. Or we could notice what's growing right in front of us. Look back at this whole week. The cup, emptied. The woman, set down at the river. Is that so. The moon that stays. The bowl, washed. The finger and the moon. And now, one strawberry. Seven Zen stories, and each one keeps pointing at the same place: right here.
screen: `A STRAWBERRY, WITHIN REACH.` · `AN OLD PARABLE: A WARNING.` · `ZEN TURNS IT AROUND.` · `SEVEN STORIES, ONE PLACE.` · then, large: `HOW SWEET IT TASTED!`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: taste one thing fully today. If you have something to eat or drink nearby, a berry, a sip of tea, a piece of bread, take it now. If not, remember the last thing you really tasted. Settle, and breathe. Put it in your mouth and don't rush. Notice the first taste, then how it changes. The texture. The temperature. Let your worries hang on the vine for a moment. They'll still be there. Just taste. The bell holds the time.
The strawberry. Between two tigers, on a vine the mice are gnawing, a man picks a wild strawberry and tastes it fully. Today's word.
screen: `THE STRAWBERRY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: how sweet it tasted. Today, find one strawberry in a crowded day and taste it all the way. That's the Zen week: the cup, the river, is that so, the moon, the bowl, the finger, the strawberry. Day forty-nine.

screen: `DAY 49 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BUTTERFLY DREAM.`
